reader.title: Attempted lynching of Patrick Simpson
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A mob tried to lynch Simpson when he arrived at Richmond under arrest and a crowd threatened him after his discharge, but he was not killed, so this was an attempted lynching (A1, A2).

A 'mob of moonshiners' tried to lynch Simpson, who was charged with murder, and a dissatisfied crowd threatened him after the court discharged him, but no one was killed; he escaped (A1, A2). It was an attempt, not a completed lynching.

The Bristol News dispatch from Fulton, N.Y. (A1) and the New York Sun paragraph (A2) agree on the core story, but the Sun item looks like a condensation of the same Fulton account, its reprints (A3, A4) add nothing, and no report from Richmond, Ky. or from 1881 was found.

summary.text: The attempted lynching of Patrick Simpson was a pair of mob threats in 1881 against a man from Fulton, New York, who had been brought to Richmond, Kentucky, under arrest after he was mistaken for a fugitive murderer named Rogers.
A mob tried to lynch him when he arrived, and after a court discharged him a crowd surrounded the court-house; he escaped on foot and reached home about the start of 1882.
Papers told it as a story of mistaken identity and a narrow escape, and none of them gave Simpson's race.

According to a dispatch from Fulton dated January 1, a man named Simpson had been murdered at Richmond by his nephew Rogers, who escaped, and descriptions of Rogers were circulated across the country.
In June Patrick Simpson, who had left Fulton four years earlier, was arrested in Columbus, Ohio, because he resembled Rogers's pictures and description.

The authorities claimed he had taken the murdered man's name to avoid detection, acquaintances of Rogers from Richmond 'positively identified' him, and he was taken to Kentucky on a requisition from the governor.
In the Bristol News version, 'a mob of moonshiners' was waiting when he reached Richmond and tried to lynch him, but the jail guard was doubled and he was saved.
He was committed three times on habeas corpus proceedings and spent several months in jail.
In October he showed that he had been in Fulton when the crime was committed, and the court accepted the proof.
After the ruling, a crowd 'dissatisfied with the decision of the court' surrounded the court-house.
His counsel hurried him into a side-building, gave him seven dollars, and told him to flee the country or he would lose his life.
Simpson hid until night, swam the Kentucky river, and made for the mountains, travelling through thickets by night and hiding by day until he was hundreds of miles from Richmond.
He reached Fulton about January 1, 1882, 'worn out with anxiety and suffering'; no arrest of anyone in the mob or the crowd is reported in the coverage.

The story appears to have started with the Fulton dispatch, which the Bristol News of Bristol, Virginia and Tennessee, printed on January 10, 1882, under the headline 'A Flight for Life' and the deck 'Mistaken for a murderer and threatened by a mob after his discharge.'

Two days later the New York Sun ran a shorter, undated version in its 'Sunbeams' column, saying a 'dissatisfied mob undertook to lynch him' and that 'the county officials were too cowardly to protect him.'

The Silver State of Unionville, Nevada, reprinted the Sun paragraph word for word on January 20, and the Semi-Weekly Interior Journal of Stanford, Kentucky, did the same on February 3 without local comment.
None of these papers mentioned race, and no account from Richmond itself was found.

The two versions differ on the mob and the officials: the Fulton dispatch describes a lynching attempt stopped by a doubled jail guard and then a hostile crowd at the court-house, while the Sun describes one mob after his release and calls the county officials cowardly.
The Fulton dispatch is the fuller and more specific of the two, and the Sun paragraph reads as a condensed version of the same story.

accounts.label: Fulton, N.Y. dispatch
accounts.gist: A mob of moonshiners tried to lynch Simpson when he arrived at Richmond but was prevented, and the doubled jail guard saved him. After his October discharge a dissatisfied crowd surrounded the court-house, and his counsel sent him away to flee for his life.

accounts.label: New York Sun paragraph
accounts.gist: Once he had convinced the authorities of the mistake, a dissatisfied mob undertook to lynch him and the county officials were too cowardly to protect him, so he escaped on foot through the woods.

framing.detail: The Bristol News headed it 'A Flight for Life' with the deck 'Mistaken for a murderer and threatened by a mob after his discharge,' telling it as an innocent man's escape.
The Sun said the county officials were 'too cowardly to protect him', blaming them for his flight.
The Silver State and the Stanford Interior Journal reprinted the Sun paragraph without comment.

record_check.dossier: June to October 1881: arrest in June, the mob attempt on his arrival soon after, discharge and the crowd at the court-house in October. Exact days are not reported, and the news ran in January-February 1882.
Not stated in any article; no racial framing appears. It is unclear that this was anti-Black violence.
